We thank reviewer iiFf for the thorough reviews, constructive suggestions, and insightful questions. We provide detailed answers to your comments below.

**weakness 1. In modern applications, it is common for optimization problems to have uncertain or unknown constraint parameters.**

We agree with the reviewer's point that our work primarily focuses on parameter uncertainty but does not yet address uncertainty in the parameters of constraints or unknown optimization objective functions. Indeed, when organizing the benchmark, we considered that methods for uncertainty in constraints (arXiv.2311.08022, aaai.v37i4.25513) are mainly based on IntOpt[1] (which falls under the continuous category we mentioned, using implicit differentiation for gradient approximation). Other predict-and-optimize methods do not currently support uncertainty in constraints. Consequently, direct cross-comparison of methods and datasets was not feasible and thus was not included in our current work. We will continue to maintain this benchmark and incorporate methods that support these scenarios into our benchmark as they become available in the future.

**weakness 2.it does not provide detailed empirical evaluations of these methods on non-linear and non-convex problems. The effectiveness and limitations of these surrogate approaches are not thoroughly analyzed.**
    

We agree with the reviewer's view that many problems are non-linear and non-convex, and surrogate-based methods are a promising direction in the past two years. We kindly remind the reviewer that we provided the evaluation results for LODL, and LODL achieved good performance on four problems. EGL's code has not yet been released，so it is not incorported in our framework for now.

Beyond the empirical experiments, we also discussed the resources required by these methods and their limitations in practical use in the comparison table (Table 1), Section 3.4, and Figure 4. We will continue to follow the progress of these methods and update our benchmark accordingly in the future.

We also believe that, just as linear and convex problems have broad applications in the current optimization field and have become major scenarios in optimization, we hope that the existing benchmark can assist the community in these areas.

**weakness 3. This reliance on synthetic data can limit the generalizability and applicability of the findings.**

We agree with your opinion that for predict-then-optimize, the practical performance gains may be more evident on real data that includes noise, and this field call for more real-world datasets and approaches that based on real dataset evaluation. 

- In our benchmark, we include six datasets from real-world scenarios: Energy Scheduling, Knapsack (Energy), Budget Allocation, Bipartite Matching, Portfolio Optimization, and Combinatorial Advertising. 

- For the Combinatorial Advertising problem we proposed, we will continue to accumulate data, maintain, and release more data for industry exploration. 

- Our current evaluation assumes that the true optimization coefficients are known, so that evaluation by regret is possible. In many real-world scenarios, many optimization coefficients are unknown during testing, making regret evaluation impossible. Instead, tasks are assessed through offline simulations (such as our Combinatorial Advertising problem) or online A/B testing, which are more challenging.

**weakness 4.The scalability of the methods to high-dimensional data sets is not thoroughly tested or discussed.**


As also mentioned in Section 4.5, RQ3, our experiments revealed that as the scale of decision variables increases, the performance of existing methods may decline, sometimes even falling below that of two-stage  (PtO) approach. In Table 7 of the appendix, we included the training and testing times for the knapsack problem as the size grows. It can be observed that the training time for some methods (e.g., LTR) increases rapidly. During the testing phase, PnO and PTO methods have no additional time overhead at the same level of complexity.

We also remind that some of the datasets we support allow for user-defined generation. For example, in the knapsack problem, datasets of any scale (including high-dimensional) can be generated.

**weakness 5.The paper does not provide sufficient analysis of failure cases where PnO methods perform poorly.**

Thanks for the reviewer's nice suggestion. We added a set of qualitative analysis on the knapsack problem to explore the reasons behind the success or failure of these methods. 
We also present in Appendix D.5 of the revised paper in the anonymous link for your further review:  https://anonymous.4open.science/r/review-E343.

For the 10-th test instance in the knapsack problem, first, we visualize the values and weights of the problem (https://ibb.co/7N8mhdS). We plot the predicted values for 20 items (https://ibb.co/nsQKQLp) for three models: the two-stage model, the well-performing SPO model, and the poorly-performing Blackbox model.

We can observe that the SPO model achieved the best decision quality (with the objective value of 18, selecting items 1, 3, 6, 9, 17, and 18). The two-stage model's decision quality was slightly lower (with the objective value of 17, selecting items 1, 3, 6, 8, 9, and 17). SPO improved decision quality by replacing item 9 with item 18, by predicting a higher predicted value to item 18 and lowering the prediction for item 9, which is guided by information of optimization objective while the two-stage does not involve this. Although this increased the prediction error, it enhanced the decision quality.

For the Blackbox model, we observed that its predicted values were similar to SPO for some items, but due to the lack of label supervision during the prediction phase (not using coefficient labels), the prediction errors were larger, leading to poorer decision quality.

We thank reviewer LjCy for the thorough reviews, constructive suggestions, and insightful questions. We provide detailed answers to your comments below.

**Weakness1: There's no dedicated related work section that delineates prior work to the proposed benchmark. some highly related works could have been addressed in greater detail.**

Due to the high overlap between our categorization (in Sec 3) and related work, we initially does not include seperate section for related work. We have now added it to the appendix, where the revised paper in the anonymous link for your further review:  https://anonymous.4open.science/r/review-E343.
    
We thank the reviewer for specifically bringing several related works to attention, and we have also included these works in the updated related work. 

-  [1,2] focus on the solving of CO problems with neural solvers, but they primarily address solving under known and fixed coefficients. We agree that combining these neural solvers with PnO methods in predictive CO is a promising direction, however integrating neural solvers into the PnO framework is not yet fully mature for the following reasons: (1) in some CO problems, most of them are still inferior to heuristic algorithms (such as the LKH in the TSP) in terms of solving efficiency and quality, and (2) these methods are often not fully differentiable (as some of them may require search algorithms to satisfy the constraints), so they still require the PnO methods we mentioned in the backward pass. 

- As for [3,4,5], these are indeed inspiring works. However, since current PnO methods do not support arbitrary uncertainty scenarios and are limited to cases with a known closed-form optimization objective but unknown coefficients, they are currently out of the scope of our benchmark. In [3,5], the form of the optimization objective function is uncertain and change with time (especially for the pickup task), and [4] focuses more on performing regression among combinatorial spaces when there is no test data distribution during training but training data generation is available. Therefore, our paper mainly focuses on methods within the predict-and-optimize paradigm, and does not include them for now.
- Regarding the relationship with reference [6], we kindly remind the reviewer to refer to the latest version of [6] on arXiv(https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07633).
- As briefly mentioned in the introduction section that [7] only supports linear or convex problems, and the methods it supports are limited. Therefore in our work, we first give a more systematic summary of this field and analysis based on comprehensive benchmark. Additionally, our benchmark specifically targets uncertainty in combinatorial optimization, where discrete decision variables may occur unique challenges.

**Weakness2: there is an opportunity for improvement in including real-world routing problem variants to broaden the scope and narrowing the gap to the current (deterministic) NCO literature that predominantly addresses CO problems in the routing domain.**

We agree with the reviewer's view that routing problems are also a representative class of CO problems. Due to the lack of publicly available TSP datasets with uncertain coefficients, we conducted experiments using simulated data: on the graph of 20 nodes, we generate the node coodinates by the uniform distribution $[0,1]$, and the edge cost $t_e$ for edge $e =(u,v)$ is Euclidean distance plus a congestion parameter:
$$t_e = D_E(x_u, x_v) * c_e + \operatorname{poly}(x_e)$$
where $x_u, x_v$ are the node coordinates of node $u$ and $v$, $D_E$ is the Euclidean distance, $c_e$ is the congestion parameter sampled from Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(1,1)$, $x_e$ is the edge features for $e$

We train on 400 instances and test on 200 instances, and our preliminary results are as follows.

|| PtO(Two-stage)|PnO(SPO)|
|-|-|-|
|Regret |82.88278|33.75459|
|Train time(second/epoch)|0.04259 |2.73619|
|Test time (second)|2.66494|1.69280|

We will also add TSP dataset to our benchmark in the near future.

**Weakness3:I would recommend extending and upgrading the base of two-stage approaches, notably ML prediction models.**

We agree with the reviewer's opinion that many existing works still use relatively simple predictive models, such as linear regression and k nearest neighbor [8,9]. We will later upgrade the benchmark to better predictive models, and we believe that in general, predict-and-optimize methods have greater potential in such tasks.

**Weakness4: The documentation with regards to the evaluation metrics and optimal objective values used in the experiments can be improved.**

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. Due to the page limit, we placed the explanation of the evaluation metrics (regret and uplift) in the appendix. We will reorganize the paper to provide more detailed information in the main paper.

We thank reviewer XAzY for the thorough reviews, constructive suggestions, and insightful questions. We provide detailed answers to your comments below.

**Q1:Could you explain whether PtO and PnO fall under neural combinatorial optimization methods, and what their main differences are?**

We have also noticed of the neural combinatorial solvers you mentioned, which are orthogonal to the predictive CO tasked that we are focusing on. The key differences between the two are as follows:

- **Neural Combinatorial Solvers**:
  - The problem setting typically assumes that the coefficients of the optimization problem (e.g., the costs associated with each path in the Traveling Salesman Problem) are known and fixed.
  - The core focus lies in designing machine learning techniques to directly solve the CO problem, where the learnable parameters are within the neural network model of the solver.

- **Predictive Combinatorial Optimization**:
  - The problem setting assumes that the coefficients of the optimization problem are unknown.
  - The main focus is on learning a predictive model that is suitable for downstream uncertain optimization tasks. The optimization solver is generally not the focus and can usually apply to any black-box solvers. The learnable parameters are concentrated in the predictive model that precedes the solver, rather than in the solver itself.
  - The PtO and PnO refer to methods for predictive CO problems.

**Q2: PnO methods directly train an end-to-end model. Is this type of method sensitive to the magnitude of optimization coefficients?**

Our recent experiments also found that these methods may be sensitive to the magnitude of the optimization parameters. On the knapsack dataset where the magnitudes of raw features $x$ and coefficients $y$ differed between the training and testing sets, both PtO and PnO shows performance decline in decision quality.

|  |Trained & tested on distribution 2|Trained on distribution 1, tested on distribution 2 |
| - | - | - | 
|Two-stage|2.395|11.220| 
|SPO|2.260|10.670|
where the setting is given as:
- Distribution 1: the raw features are generated by Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(10,10)$
- Distribution 2: the raw features are generated by Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$

The data generation process are the same as used in our benchmark. In this case, the optimization coefficients may differ by 100 or even 1,000 times. We observed from the results that when the distribution changes, the decision quality can significantly decline.

**Q3: Are the results in Table 3 from a single run or the average of multiple independent runs?**

Our experiments are based on a single run. Since the solver is called after the prediction module, the experimental results of the decision task under our predictive co-task are relatively stable, which is different from traditional pure prediction tasks in machine learning.

**Q4: The content in Figure 2 is difficult to understand. It is suggested that the authors reorganize the content of Figure 2.**

Thanks for the reviewer's suggestion. As gradient propagation is central to predictive CO problems, Figure 2 visualizes the gradients between the original input ( $x$ ), optimization coefficient ( $y$ ), and the final solution ( $z$ ) for the existing PtO and PnO methods. This visualization aims to aid readers in better understanding the existing methods and the basis for our categorization. We will also include additional texts to further explain this figure.

**Q5: Some images lack labels, such as the x-axis in Figure 7. Additionally, the placement of some images and tables is too far from the relevant text.**

Thank you for your suggestion. The x-axis in Figure 7 represents relative regret (total regret/total optimal value). We will revise the paper accordingly.

We thank reviewer tYMG for the thorough reviews, constructive suggestions, and insightful questions. We provide detailed answers to your comments below.

**Q1: "there is no silver bullet found for the specific design choices of PnO".  what would be value of this benchmarking project?**

We thank the reviewer for your valuable feedback. We would clarify that, just as the choice of solving methods for optimization problems depends on the specific problem form (e.g., simplex for linear programming, interior-point methods for constrained problems), we have found that predict-and-optimize models (not just solvers) for predictive CO problems also present different characteristics and requirements (as shown in Table 1) and are suited to different problems (as illustrated in Figure 4). Based on the findings from our benchmark experiments, no single model performs best across all problems, leading us to the title that "there is no silver bullet."

Nevertheless, our benchmark aims to benefit the academic community to more easily evaluate new algorithms, and it can also serve as a reference for industrial deployment (we have also provided suggestions for industrial deployment in Sec 3.5). The pipeline in our benchmark is **clearly defined and unified** for various methods. As shown in Figure 3, we can decouple predictor, solver, and predict-and-optimize methods (denoted losses in the figure). Community developers can easily replace in any of these modules and conduct the experiments they need.

title.value: The submission provides a comprehensive review and classification of predictive combinatorial optimization methods, testing their performance on various problems. Overall, the paper is well-written and makes a valuable contribution to the field.

summary_and_contributions.value: The main contribution of this paper lies in testing two types of methods, Predict-then-Optimize and Predict-and-Optimize, on a series of problems to evaluate their performance in predictive combinatorial optimization, while also exploring some key factors for Predict-and-Optimize methodology design.

review.value:
This paper focuses on a specific type of combinatorial optimization problem, the predictive combinatorial optimization problem. The authors detail the advantages and disadvantages of two types of methods, PtO and PnO, providing a systematic summary and classification of existing methods. Additionally, the performance of these methods are tested on a series of problems. Impressively, the authors also provide a new test problem based on real-world application scenarios, laying a solid foundation for the development of this research direction.
I think the topic studied in this paper is very important and meaningful. However, I have the following questions:
1. For traditional combinatorial optimization problems, in addition to exact methods and heuristic methods, there is also a class of neural combinatorial optimization methods. Could you explain whether PtO and PnO fall under neural combinatorial optimization methods, and what their main differences are?
2. PnO methods directly train an end-to-end model. Is this type of method sensitive to the magnitude of optimization coefficients?
3. Are the results in Table 3 from a single run or the average of multiple independent runs?
4. The content in Figure 2 is difficult to understand. It is suggested that the authors reorganize the content of Figure 2.
5. Some images lack labels, such as the x-axis in Figure 7. Additionally, the placement of some images and tables is too far from the relevant text.

strengths.value: The background of the problem is clearly explained, various methods are comprehensively summarized, and experiments are extensive and well-reasoned.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: The article lacks detailed descriptions of compared algorithms.

limitations.value: It is suggested that the authors consider the performance of various methods in the context of small datasets in future research, where objective evaluation is expensive and only a limited amount of training data can be collected.

correctness.value: The claims made in the submission are correct.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Yes, the authors not only explored the performance of different methods but also provided some algorithm design tips, further enhancing the practical application prospects of these methods.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper reviews existing “predict-and-optimize” (“PnO”) methodologies for predictive combinatorial optimization and categorizes these methods into four categories according to the characteristics of decision variables. title.value: Comprehensive Benchmark for Predicitve Combinatorial Optimization and a new real-world dataset

summary_and_contributions.value:
The paper proposes a benchmark and modular code base for Predictive Combinatorial Optimization (CO), as well as a novel industrial combinatorial advertising (CA) dataset. The authors include a review and categorization of state-of-the-art (SotA) predict-and-optimize (PnO) approaches in the field and explain the potential drawbacks of the previously applied Predict-then-Optimize (PtO) paradigm.
Extensive experiments are performed on 7 publicly available datasets and a separate smaller experiment is performed on the newly introduced CA dataset. Concerning the baselines, 10 PnO approaches are selected, while only a single 2-stage-approach is benchmarked.
The experimental results are analyzed along three research questions that aim at guiding the design and versatility of future PnO approaches.

review.value:
The problem tackled in the paper is well motivated and the contributions are well formulated. In general, the paper is well written and the claims are correct.
The paper provides a useful categorization of current SotA PnO methods in summary (Table 1) as well as in a more detailed aspect concerning the different loss functions decision variable types used (section 3). 

A dedicated related work section is missing, even though chapter 1 mentions prior work. A clearer delineation to existing work would have been beneficial.

The experiments seem rather extensive and cover the typical CO problems tackled in the predictive CO field. 
Nevertheless, different types of CO problems, that currently are not predominantly handled in the predictive CO, but rather in the Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) literature, such as routing problem variants, could have been an interesting and useful addition. 
Especially given that most of the coefficients of such routing problems in real-world scenarios are unknown at the time of decision making ([3], [4], [5]).
Even if most neural solvers in the NCO literature (e.g. [1], [2]) look at determinstic versions of the CO problems, these approaches - in combination - with a (first-stage-) predictive model, could have functioned as useful ML baselines here.
Furthermore, given that the experimental results are not entirely conclusive in terms that PnO approaches are superior to the PtO strategy, I would have liked to see a variety of strong PtO baselines, especially considering that the concurrently used predictive model consists of a fairly weak two-layer MLP and it is also not clear which solver is used for the two-stage approach in the experiments. 

The proposed novel dataset concerning combinatorial advertising is a useful extension to the current pool of typical CO problems handled in the field of predictive CO. Appendix B.7.2. covers important meta-data regarding the dataset.

Concerning the analysis of the experimental results along the three research questions; 
Some artifacts are not clearly disentangled, such as the fact that a higher prediction loss in the training of PnO methods leads to better error trade-offs via information of decision objectives (line 299-301).
Furthermore some research questions are only addressed for single CO problems (s.a. RQ1 for the real-world knapsack problem), while given the diverse performances in Table 3, looking at the results for a single CO problem, might not lead to conclusive results.


References:
[1] Chen, Jinbiao, et al. "Efficient meta neural heuristic for multi-objective combinatorial optimization." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (2024).
[2] Hertrich, Christoph, and Martin Skutella. "Provably good solutions to the knapsack problem via neural networks of bounded size." INFORMS journal on computing 35.5 (2023): 1079-1097.
[3] Joe, Waldy, and Hoong Chuin Lau. "Deep reinforcement learning approach to solve dynamic vehicle routing problem with stochastic customers." Proceedings of the international conference on automated planning and scheduling. Vol. 30. 2020.
[4] Tong, Guangmo. "Usco-solver: Solving undetermined stochastic combinatorial optimization problems." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 1646-1659.
[5] Zhou, Chenhao, et al. "Reinforcement Learning-based approach for dynamic vehicle routing problem with stochastic demand." Computers & Industrial Engineering 182 (2023): 109443.
[6] Geng, Haoyu, et al. "Rethinking and Benchmarking Predict-then-Optimize Paradigm for Combinatorial Optimization Problems." arXiv preprint arXiv:2311.07633 (2023).
[7] Tang, Bo, and Elias B. Khalil. "Pyepo: A pytorch-based end-to-end predict-then-optimize library for linear and integer programming." Mathematical Programming Computation (2024): 1-39.

strengths.value:
The main strength of the contribution is the thorough analytical review and categorization of current approaches as well as the modularity of the code base that supports and potentially boosts the development of novel approaches in the field.
Moreover, the practical approach in analyzing the results in the experimental section and notably section 3.5 demonstrates relevance for the broader research community and specifically facilitates the transfer between research and industry concerning solutions to real-world problems.
The proposed combinatorial advertising dataset, albeit fairly specific and non-generic, introduces a challenging real-world problem where coefficient labels are not present.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
There's no dedicated related work section that delineates prior work to the proposed benchmark, while prior work is mentioned in chapter 1 some highly related works ([6], [7] see references above) could have been addressed in greater detail.
Especially the relation to the work in [6] that appears to propose a new combinatorial advertising dataset as well and benchmarks PtO approaches should have been highlighted.
Even though the authors claim that the selection of CO problems is representative of currently addressed problems in the field, I would argue that there is an opportunity for improvement in including real-world routing problem variants to broaden the scope and narrowing the gap to the current (deterministic) NCO literature that predominantly addresses CO problems in the routing domain.
Furthermore, as mentioned above, I would recommend extending and upgrading the base of two-stage approaches, notably ML prediction models, to clarify whether PnO approaches outperform PtO on the CO problems other then Portfolio Optimization and Cubic Top-K problem, where the PtO approaches demonstrate good performances.
The documentation with regards to the evaluation metrics and optimal objective values used in the experiments can be improved.

limitations.value: Limitations and broader impacts are stated and adequately addressed in Appendix D.

correctness.value: The claims in the submission seem correct. The evaluation is correctly performed and the experiments are (too a great extent) reproducible, since code is provided in terms of a anonymous github repository.

clarity.value:
In general the paper is well written, some minor points:

- Table 5 in line 265 is labeled as Figure 5.
- Figure 3 appears before Figure 2 on page 4

relation_to_prior_work.value: The authors mention related benchmarks/datasets in the motivational section (chapter 1), even though there's no dedicated related work section.

documentation.value:
Details concerning the dataset are clearly documented in appendix B.7, while details concerning maintenance, responsible use, hosting and licensing plans are listed in appendix D. There's no URL for reviewers to access the dataset.

The performance metrics (relative regret (%) and uplift) should be explained in the main text, as well as the details on the solver used to obtain the optimal objective for each of the CO problems and the solver used in the 2-stage approach.

ethics.value: No ethical concerns. Notes on privacy are detailed in Appendix D.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value: With regards to the related work, a delineation to the related stream of research regarding Neural Combinatorial Optimization, that albeit is concerned mostly with deterministic routing problem variants, could have been included. To this end, I would suggest to include determinstic NCO approaches in combination with predictive models for future versions and extensions of the benchmark.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper provides a systematic empirical evaluation of various Predict-and-Optimize (PnO) and Predict-then-Optimize (PtO) methods. It introduces a modular framework to benchmark 11 different PtO/PnO methods across 8 distinct combinatorial optimization problems, including a new industrial dataset for combinatorial advertising. The results indicate that PnO methods generally outperform PtO methods, although no single method consistently performs best across all scenarios.

review.value:
**Strengths:**

1.The paper offers a broad empirical evaluation of 11 PtO/PnO methods on 8 distinct combinatorial optimization problems, providing a valuable benchmark for researchers and practitioners in the field.

2.The inclusion of a new industrial dataset for combinatorial advertising enhances the practical relevance of the study and provides a valuable resource for future research.

3.The categorization of existing methods into discrete, continuous, statistical, and surrogate categories helps in understanding the landscape of PnO/PtO approaches and guides the selection of appropriate methods for specific problems.

**Weaknesses:**

1.The paper assumes that the coefficients of the constraints are known in line with the majority of literature [57, 50, 34]. However, they are no longer the latest literature. In modern applications, it is common for optimization problems to have uncertain or unknown constraint parameters. This strong assumption limits the applicability of the findings to real-world problems where such uncertainty is prevalent. ​For example, the literature (https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2311.08022, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v37i4.25513) has discussed related problems.

2.Real-world problems are often non-linear and non-convex. While the paper does mention surrogate methods like LODL and EGL that aim to handle non-linear objectives by converting them into linear forms, it does not provide detailed empirical evaluations of these methods on non-linear and non-convex problems. The effectiveness and limitations of these surrogate approaches are not thoroughly analyzed.

3.While the paper introduces a new industrial dataset for combinatorial advertising, the overall variety and realism of the datasets used in the experiments are limited. Many datasets are synthetically generated, which may not capture the complexity and variability of real-world data. This reliance on synthetic data can limit the generalizability and applicability of the findings. Real-world datasets often contain noise, outliers, and other irregularities that are not adequately represented in synthetic datasets.

4.The scalability of the methods to high-dimensional data sets is not thoroughly tested or discussed. High-dimensional optimization problems are common in fields like finance, healthcare, and logistics, where the number of variables and constraints can be very large. The paper does not provide sufficient evidence or benchmarks to demonstrate that the proposed methods can handle such high-dimensional problems efficiently.

5.The paper does not provide sufficient analysis of failure cases where PnO methods perform poorly. Understanding the conditions and reasons for failure is crucial for improving and refining these methods. Detailed case studies and error analyses are missing, which would help in identifying the limitations and potential areas for enhancement of the methods​.

6.The paper acknowledges the challenges in deploying PnO methods in real-world industrial settings but does not delve deeply into these challenges or propose concrete solutions. For instance, integrating these methods into existing systems and managing the computational overhead are significant concerns that are not thoroughly addressed. This lack of practical guidance may hinder the adoption of PnO methods in industry.

title.value: Benchmarking PtO and PnO Methods in the Predictive Combinatorial Optimization Regime

abstract.value: Predictive combinatorial optimization, where the parameters of combinatorial optimization (CO) are unknown at the decision-making time, is the precise modeling of many real-world applications, including energy cost-aware scheduling and budget allocation on advertising. Tackling such a problem usually involves a prediction model and a CO solver. These two modules are integrated into the predictive CO pipeline following two design principles: ''Predict-then-Optimize (PtO)'', which learns predictions by supervised training and subsequently solves CO using predicted coefficients, while the other, named ''Predict-and-Optimize (PnO)'', directly optimizes towards the ultimate decision quality and claims to yield better decisions than traditional PtO approaches. However, there lacks a systematic benchmark of both approaches, including the specific design choices at the module level, as well as an evaluation dataset that covers representative real-world scenarios. To this end, we develop a modular framework to benchmark 11 existing PtO/PnO methods on 8 problems, including a new industrial dataset for combinatorial advertising that will be released. Our study shows that PnO approaches are better than PtO on 7 out of 8 benchmarks, but there is no silver bullet found for the specific design choices of PnO. A comprehensive categorization of current approaches and integration of typical scenarios are provided under a unified benchmark. Therefore, this paper could serve as a comprehensive benchmark for future PnO approach development and also offer fast prototyping for application-focused development. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/PredictiveCO-Benchmark}.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
